title: AI agent skills: One library for humans and AI agents | Pylon
summary: Give every human and AI teammate the same playbook. Learn how to turn support know-how into a shared AI agent skill library your whole team can use.
body_markdown:
When your team changes how it investigates API timeouts, that new process needs to reach everyone involved in the next report. But the instructions might live scattered between a support document, an engineer’s notes, and a saved AI prompt. Updating only the document means team members and[AI agents](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/how-to-use-ai-agents) will likely follow different versions of the same process.


[AI agent skills](https://www.usepylon.com/ai-agents/skills) give you a way to centralize and standardize important support work. With[Pylon’s agentic platform](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/pylon-becomes-the-agentic-support-platform) , your B2B support team can use shared instructions to guide their own workflows and those of AI agents.


In this guide, we’ll discuss what AI agent skills are and how they work. We’ll also explain how you can build these instructions from existing resources, then keep improving them as your product and support needs change.


## What are AI agent skills?


Ask AI view from Pylon


A skill is a reusable set of instructions that teaches an AI agent how to complete a specific task. Broad agent skills format and package procedural knowledge, so the AI can access useful guidance when it needs to complete work.


For your support team, this might mean building an API investigation skill that specifies which details to collect when a request comes in, what sources to check, how to identify a solution, and when to[escalate the ticket](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/escalation-tools-customer-support) to engineering.


These skills can provide guidance for human team members too, so both your team and AI agents work from the same best practices. A teammate could follow the process manually or ask an agent to run it; either way, everyone is on the same page about what a complete investigation needs.


## Why B2B support teams need one shared skill library


As you adopt[agentic AI to improve support](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/agentic-ai-use-cases) , it becomes more important to maintain consistent instructions. Without a shared process, changes can drift across separate team runbooks and AI setups.


If engineering adds a required diagnostic field, you might update the onboarding document but miss the prompt a teammate uses to prepare escalations. As a result, the next handoff could lack some of the information engineering needs. In contrast, a shared agent skill library keeps customer context and updates in the same place.


## How to build an AI agent skill library for your support team: 7 steps


To learn how to create an AI agent skill, start with a single process you can explain and evaluate clearly. Then, you’ll turn that process into guidance your team and AI agents can rely on. Here’s how.


### 1. Identify workflows worth turning into skills


AI saves the most time when used for repeat tasks, so look for common investigations or[triage decisions](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-support-triage) with straightforward inputs and outcomes. Narrow your focus to one workflow, and look for knowledge gaps and missing or inconsistent steps that could be handled more efficiently by AI.


### 2. Document the process in everyday language


Describe the evidence the AI needs to collect, the goal it should work toward, the checks it will perform, and the expected output. In some tools, the skill’s description also helps the agent decide when to load its instructions.


For our API timeout example, you might want the AI to review the affected endpoint, the request time, and any relevant logs, then give a summary of what’s still unknown. Keep the instructions specific enough that a teammate could follow them as well.


### 3. Define the skill’s triggers and scope


State the symptoms that make the skill relevant and the situations it excludes, then choose which teams and agents can use it. As you[set up AI agents](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/how-to-set-up-ai-agents) , Pylon lets you scope skills and limit their availability to individual agents.


Check each agent’s tools separately, and define what it should do when a required source is unavailable. For instance, you could have it return a partial evidence summary with a request for human investigation.


### 4. Build the skill from a real ticket


Work through an issue using an[Assist Agent](https://www.usepylon.com/ai-agents/assist) , refining the investigation and output steps as you go. Once you’re happy with your workflow, you can ask the Assist Agent to turn it into a skill.


Review the generated instructions to remove customer-specific details and assumptions specific to the original issue. One successful resolution gives you a starting point to build on, not proof that the skill will handle every variation perfectly.


### 5. Assign an accountable owner


Choose someone on your team who understands the workflow and can handle questions about it. That person should coordinate changes with engineering and product teams when dependencies change. For our API investigation skill, an endpoint update or a new logging system could call for a revision, even if the support policy stays the same.


### 6. Roll the skill out to your team and AI


As your team learns how to use AI agents for repeat support work, have both teammates and AI agents practice the instructions on representative issues. Compare the evidence gathered and look for missing information or poor escalation decisions.


Be sure to include a case with incomplete inputs or unavailable tools, so you know how the skill functions under less-than-ideal conditions. And always check the actual handoff or updated record, instead of relying on a completion message.


### 7. Set a review cadence


Review the skill on a regular schedule and after relevant product or policy changes. Pylon can surface suggested updates based on how skills perform, so your team can review and apply those changes as needed. After a change, rerun the cases that exposed the problem to see if the new instructions fix the issue without disrupting other workflows.


## What makes an AI skill effective


Agent runbook view from Pylon


Once you’ve tested a skill, use these criteria to decide whether it belongs in your shared library. A good skill should have:


- **One clear outcome.** Define what completion looks like, such as an engineering handoff with reproduction steps and linked evidence. Split unrelated tasks into separate skills so the agent can select the right one.
- **Readable instructions.** Write instructions in the same language your team uses to explain the job. A support lead should be able to identify an outdated step without decoding a dev’s shorthand.
- **Specific trigger conditions.** Describe the situations where the skill applies, including relevant symptoms. Add exclusions, so an API performance investigation skill isn’t chosen for an unrelated access question.
- **A named owner.** Make it clear who approves changes and answers questions. When a teammate finds a missing step, they should know where to send that feedback.
- **An appropriate audience.** Shared instructions should preserve the process, but internal findings and customer replies need different outputs. Pylon’s[Support Agents](https://www.usepylon.com/ai-agents/support) use approved public knowledge in answers, so internal logs and investigation notes should stay internal.
- **A workable review schedule.** Choose a review cadence that matches how often the workflow changes. Retire skills that depend on older features or processes to avoid confusing agents.
- **Portable, explicit dependencies.** Pylon can[import existing skill markdown files](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/agents/skills) from other AI tools, but an imported instruction doesn’t bring tool access with it. Verify that the receiving agent can perform each step, then adapt any tool-specific details.

## FAQ


### Do support teams need engineers to build AI agent skills?


No code is required to write the instructions for an AI agent skill. Support managers and team leads can create and refine skills in everyday language, although custom tools or integrations may need engineering help.


### How do you create a skill for an AI agent?


To create an AI agent skill, describe the outcome, steps, sources, and permitted actions. In Pylon, you can work through an API issue with Assist Agent, turn that workflow into a skill, then review and test it before making it available to the intended teammates and agents.


### How do I know if a workflow is a good candidate for an AI agent skill?


To find the right workflow for an AI agent skill, look for a repetitive, well-defined task with a clear start and end. A new teammate should be able to follow the process from written instructions and recognize when to ask for help.
